mcqs.question: Why does offset-based pagination (records 100-120) tend to break for a feed specifically, more visibly than for a mostly-static dataset?
options: Offset-based pagination is always slower than cursor-based pagination regardless of data volatility
New posts arriving between requests shift every subsequent offset, causing items to be skipped or duplicated as the user scrolls
Offset-based pagination cannot be implemented on a mobile client at all
This only affects feeds with fewer than 100 total posts
mcqs.explanation: A feed's content changes between requests as new posts arrive, and offset pagination's fixed numeric position shifts underneath that change, producing skipped or duplicated items — cursor-based pagination anchors to a specific item instead, which is stable against insertions elsewhere in the list. This isn't purely a speed issue, it's fully implementable on mobile, and it isn't gated on total post count.

mcqs.question: A feed's page-merge logic appends every post returned by a fresh page fetch onto the cached list without checking for duplicates. What real-world scenario can cause a visible duplicate post in the UI?
options: This can never actually happen if the API is implemented correctly
A post being deleted between two of the user's requests can shift a cursor's position slightly, causing the same post to appear in two overlapping page fetches
Duplicates only occur if the user has a slow network connection
This is exclusively a database indexing bug, unrelated to the merge logic
mcqs.explanation: Real-world churn in the underlying feed — a post deleted between requests, for instance — can cause overlapping page fetches to return the same post twice, which a naive append-everything merge doesn't catch; de-duplicating by ID during the merge is what actually prevents the visible duplicate. This is a real, common scenario, not something that 'correct' API implementation alone eliminates, and it's unrelated to connection speed or database indexing specifically.

mcqs.question: A popular post's like count is changing constantly from other users' activity, independent of this user's own like action. How should the client display the count after this user optimistically likes it?
options: Overwrite the displayed count entirely with the next fetched server value, discarding the user's own optimistic increment
Freeze the displayed count at the moment of the user's like and never update it again
Display serverCount + localDelta, tracking this user's own optimistic change separately from the independently-drifting server count
Ignore the user's own like entirely until the next full feed refresh
mcqs.explanation: Tracking the user's own delta separately and adding it to the last-known server count avoids both erasing the user's own optimistic action and erasing other users' likes that arrived independently — overwriting with a fetched value or freezing the count entirely would lose one side or the other of this genuinely two-part problem.

mcqs.question: A background refresh detects new posts are available while the user is actively scrolling mid-feed. What's the recommended way to surface this, rather than silently inserting the new content?
options: Silently insert the new posts above the user's current scroll position immediately
Show a non-disruptive 'N new posts' banner the user can tap, rather than reordering content underneath their current scroll position
Force the app to scroll the user back to the top automatically to show the new content
Discard the new posts entirely until the user manually pulls to refresh
mcqs.explanation: A tappable banner respects the user's current position and gives them explicit control over when to see new content, avoiding the jarring experience of silently reordering or reinserting content mid-scroll. Silent insertion or a forced scroll-to-top both disrupt the user's current reading position without consent, and discarding the new posts entirely wastes a legitimate content update the user might want to see on their own terms.

mcqs.question: A user taps like, sees the button fill in immediately, then watches it briefly revert to unliked before re-filling a moment later. What's the most likely cause?
options: The like button has a rendering bug unrelated to any data synchronization

An unrelated background feed refresh fetched a server snapshot that hadn't yet reflected this user's still-in-flight like, and overwrote the optimistic state before the like's own confirmation arrived
The user's device lost network connectivity during the tap
This is expected, unavoidable behavior for any optimistic UI implementation
mcqs.explanation: The flicker happens when merge logic trusts a freshly-fetched server snapshot over a still-pending local optimistic action for the same post — the fix is treating an in-flight optimistic action as authoritative for that post until its own confirmation or rejection arrives, rather than letting an unrelated refresh overwrite it. This is a specific, avoidable race condition, not an inherent property of optimistic UI, a rendering-only bug, or a connectivity issue.

mcqs.question: A feed app discards its cached scroll position and re-fetches from page 1 every time it's reopened, forcing users to re-scroll past everything they already saw. What's the fix, while still allowing the user to intentionally refresh to the top?
options: Remove pull-to-refresh entirely so users can never accidentally lose their place

Persist the cached pages and the user's scroll position (or last-visible post ID) across sessions, restoring to that point on reopen, while keeping an explicit refresh action available for when the user wants to jump to the top
Cache only the first page and accept that scrolled-past content will always need re-fetching
Automatically scroll to the newest content on every app open, since that's what most users want
mcqs.explanation: Persisting both cached content and position, restoring to it automatically, while keeping an explicit user-initiated refresh path preserves both correctness (not losing the user's place) and control (the user can still choose to jump to the top). Removing pull-to-refresh loses a useful feature to fix an unrelated bug, caching only page one doesn't solve the scroll-position problem at all, and automatically jumping to the newest content on every open reintroduces the exact behavior causing the complaint.
